newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lithuania restates goal of NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania restates goal of NATO membership.

text.p: Lithuanian President Algirdas Brazauskas on Wednesday strongly restated the former Soviet republic's goal of being one of the first countries allowed into an expanded North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).

"Lithuania should be among the first new members... Lithuania is ready to be a reliable and active member. You should not expect us to be troublemakers," he said at a meeting with the Atlantic Alliance's 16 ambassadors in Brussels.
NATO is expected to invite some countries of former communist central and eastern Europe to join the alliance at a special summit next year.

Russia strongly opposes this eastwards expansion. Analysts predict that a deal will be struck to allow at least Poland, the Czech republic and Hungary to join, but that Moscow would baulk at the prospect of the Baltic states joining its Cold War foe.

Recalling that his country had been barred from normal relations with western Europe after its forced annexation into the Soviet Union under the 1940 Moscow-Nazi pact, Brazauskas made an emotional appeal to NATO to make good an historic wrong.

"Just now, we have a chance to ensure that the freedom of our country is not questioned in the future. We want and should take advantage of it. We need to restore the historic justice, to guarantee the independence, to return to the community of like-minded nations," he said.
Brazauskas, who is also to meet top EU officials while in Brussels, said Lithuania's bid for membership of the two organisations was part of the same process of integration with the democratic world.
"Membership is the only way for us to return to the community of western nations which share the common values of democracy, individual freedom and the rule of law," he said.
NATO officials said Brazauskas had also reiterated his country's willingness to take part in an upgraded Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme.

Alliance states increasingly see an enhanced PFP, originally set up to fill a security vacuum created by the collapse of communism, as a way of meeting the concerns of countries left out of the first, and possibly last, round of NATO enlargement.
The United States also wants the European Union to make quicker progress with EU enlargement to ease the concerns of countries such as the Baltic states.
